alt: Five family diagrams. Nuclear: parents and children. Vertically extended: three generations stacked. Horizontally extended: two brothers and their wives side by side. Single parent: one parent and children. Reconstituted: a couple with a child from a previous relationship. Below, alternatives such as communes, living alone, foster care and children’s homes.
caption: Vertical extension adds generations; horizontal extension adds relatives of the same generation.

alt: A table comparing three perspectives. Parsons: primary socialisation and stabilising adult personalities, with the nuclear family fitting industrial society; criticised by Laslett. Engels: monogamy arose with private property and families act as agents of social control. Oakley: women did most housework. Each column ends with a criticism.
caption: Each perspective has a named sociologist, a key argument and a criticism.

alt: Four cause-and-effect rows. Contraception, women’s education and work, and the cost of children lead to falling birth rates. Better nutrition, water, sanitation, vaccination and healthcare lead to falling death rates. Longer lives and fewer births lead to ageing populations such as Japan’s. Moving for work leads to internal and international migration.
caption: Each demographic change has causes you must be able to explain.

alt: A timeline of China’s population policy: a one-child policy from 1980, replaced by a two-child policy in 2016 and a three-child policy in 2021. The one-child policy reduced family size and contributed to an ageing population. Divorce laws, welfare benefits and childcare also shape families.
caption: Government policy can change family size, as China’s policies show.

alt: Left: Parsons’ traditional roles, the instrumental male breadwinner and the expressive, caring female. Right: the triple shift of paid work, domestic work and emotional work carried by many women. Below, men often make the biggest financial decisions, and Dobash and Dobash link domestic violence to male power.
caption: Many women now carry three loads: paid work, domestic work and emotional work.

alt: A three-mark answer as three linked steps: families teach children to obey parental authority; this prepares them to accept employers and the state; this keeps an unequal capitalist society stable.
caption: One point, developed in three linked steps, earns all three marks.

alt: Four steps rising from left to right: identify or name needs a brief point; describe gives features with detail; explain gives a developed reason; discuss or evaluate weighs more than one side and reaches a judgement.
caption: The command word tells you how far to develop your answer.
